title: Inference, Selection, and Simulation
purpose: This book connects population arguments to sampling evidence. It covers conditioning, randomized contrasts, partial identification, competing rates, extremum estimators, simulation error, generated objects, spectral uncertainty, dependent-data covariance, bootstrap frontiers, and out-of-time validation.
parts: Conditional Probability, Design, and Partial Identification

chapters.part: Conditional Probability, Design, and Partial Identification
chapters.title: Conditional Probability and a Model's Information Structure
chapters.overview: Probability calculations must follow the information generated by the model. Conditioning, marginalization, selection, and transformations can change expectations and variances even when marginal distributions look familiar. Independence, conditional independence, and mean independence support different algebraic steps.
chapters.method: In a discrete model where selection depends on a latent shock, calculate unconditional and selected conditional means directly from the joint table. Apply total expectation and total variance, and identify the exact restriction used whenever a product expectation is factorized.
chapters.exercise: Build a joint probability table for a shock, an action, and a selected sample indicator. Compare conditioning, marginalization, and post-selection distributions under several selection rules.
chapters.checkpoint: Annotate every expectation factorization with the independence or mean-independence condition that licenses it.
chapters.scope: The chapter states and applies the measure-theoretic results needed by the models. A separate course in measure theory is unnecessary.

chapters.part: Conditional Probability, Design, and Partial Identification
chapters.title: Symmetry, Order Statistics, and Endogenous Selection
chapters.overview: An odd statistic has zero expectation under central symmetry when its index is fixed. If the index is selected using the same shocks, the composed statistic may lose that symmetry. Order-statistic calculations and joint reflection conditions reveal the missing step.
chapters.method: For a fixed k, verify sign reversal under shock reflection. Then let K depend on the sample and derive a three-agent construction in which the selected statistic equals minus the absolute median. Compare finite-market joint reflection with a large-market selected-share limit.
chapters.exercise: Simulate samples of sizes three and five. Estimate fixed-index and selected-index expectations, attach Monte Carlo standard errors, and compare them with exact order-statistic calculations.
chapters.checkpoint: A sign claim for a selected moment requires the joint law of shocks and the selected count, not marginal shock symmetry alone.
chapters.scope: The chapter ends with LLN and quantile calculations used by the selection argument. General empirical-process theory lies outside this book.

chapters.part: Conditional Probability, Design, and Partial Identification
chapters.title: Random Assignment and Dynamic Policy Contrasts
chapters.overview: Policy effects depend on the assignment unit, timing, history, availability, and interference structure. ITT, factorial effects, sequential contrasts, and loop experiments therefore require separate estimands and assignment probabilities. Selection and nonresponse define further observation rules.
chapters.method: Derive inverse-probability contrasts for a 2-by-2 experiment and a two-stage history-dependent design. Extend the bookkeeping to cluster-assigned loops and state which target belongs to each randomization level.
chapters.exercise: Generate a synthetic micro-randomized trial and a cluster loop experiment with history-dependent availability. Recover the declared contrasts using known assignment probabilities.
chapters.checkpoint: Keep observational prediction gains separate from causal identification delivered by randomized policy loops and terminal probes.
chapters.scope: The chapter covers assignment and sampling designs used in applied economic research. Field operations and encyclopedic treatment-effect methods remain outside its boundary.

chapters.part: Conditional Probability, Design, and Partial Identification
chapters.title: Moment Inequalities, Partial Identification, and Sharp Bounds
chapters.overview: Economic optimality conditions can produce inequalities rather than equations. Validity determines the population identified set, optimization gives target extrema, and constructive witnesses establish sharpness. Sampling uncertainty is projected onto this population geometry as a separate step.
chapters.method: Derive one moment inequality from an agent's optimal choice. Form a linear program for target bounds under incomplete support and construct a primal feasible distribution at each endpoint to verify sharpness.
chapters.exercise: Compute the feasible set and target interval for a small choice model. Remove assumptions one at a time and record changes in feasibility, width, and sampling uncertainty.
chapters.checkpoint: Diagnose an empty feasible set, a wide identified set, and imprecise sample moments as three different problems.
chapters.scope: The treatment reaches validity, sharp bounds, and confidence-set projection used in the applications. General optimal moment-selection tests are omitted.

chapters.title: Stochastic Orders and Competing Sample Sizes
chapters.overview: Asymptotic negligibility depends on the normalization used by the estimator. Several sample sizes can grow at different rates, so convergence of a raw error term does not determine its contribution after root-n scaling. Triangular arrays and counterexample sequences make those comparisons explicit.
chapters.method: For n = m^4, n_I = m, and n_s = m^3, compute n/n_s^2 and n/(n_I n_s). Generalize the calculation to exponent triples and classify regimes in which bias, centered simulation variance, or sampling noise dominates.
chapters.exercise: Plot a grid of growth-rate exponents and label the dominant error term. Add boundary sequences that satisfy one published rate while violating the rate required by a root-n expansion.
chapters.checkpoint: Whenever e_n tends to zero, also evaluate the normalized sequence, such as sqrt(n)e_n, that enters the estimator's limit.
chapters.scope: The book uses finite-dimensional triangular-array reasoning. General weak convergence for stochastic processes is beyond the required toolkit.

chapters.title: Extremum Estimators and Uniform Local Expansions
chapters.overview: An optimization result, statistical consistency, and an asymptotic linear representation answer different questions. Extremum estimation requires a population criterion, uniform approximation, local curvature, controlled generated objects, and numerical tolerances that vanish on the correct scale.
chapters.method: Linearize a smooth two-step estimator around its population optimum. Display the score, Hessian, first-stage contribution, and solver remainder with their dimensions and rates. Identify how singular curvature or failed uniformity changes the expansion.
chapters.exercise: For one synthetic criterion, vary sample size and solver tolerance independently. Decompose parameter error into sampling, first-stage, and optimization components.
chapters.checkpoint: A solver's convergence certificate establishes a numerical property of the sample problem; consistency and a normal limit require statistical arguments.
chapters.scope: The chapter covers local expansions for common generated economic objects. General semiparametric empirical-process theory is omitted.

chapters.title: An Error Ledger for Monte Carlo and Forward Simulation
chapters.overview: Simulation enters as numerical integration, forward value approximation, nested averaging, and optimization input. Centered simulation noise, bias, discretization, and common-random-number dependence scale differently. A useful computation reports each component against the estimator's statistical normalization.
chapters.method: Under independent inequalities and draws, derive conditions giving centered variance of order 1/(n_I n_s). Recalculate the covariance under shared random numbers and preserve any directional simulation bias as a separate term.
chapters.exercise: Run independent and shared-random-number simulations with several values of n_I and n_s. Report variance, rate, seed sensitivity, and computation time.
chapters.checkpoint: Averaging more inequalities reduces centered noise under suitable independence; a common directional bias requires its own rate condition.
chapters.scope: The focus is forward simulation for dynamic economic estimators. MCMC and stochastic-differential-equation simulation are outside this book.

chapters.title: Kinks, Binding Inequalities, and Simulation Inference
chapters.overview: Squared violations and other kinked criteria behave differently at binding and slack moments. Centered simulation noise changes covariance, while mass at the kink can create a mean shift. The limit depends on the relative simulation rate summarized by kappa.
chapters.method: Use a bounded one-player example to calculate the score mean and variance. Derive the normalized limit for zero, finite positive, and divergent kappa, while keeping the binding-moment bias channel explicit.
chapters.exercise: Combine binding and slack moments under three computational budget sequences. Compare centered distributions, mean shifts, and standard-error formulas.
chapters.checkpoint: A covariance correction addresses centered simulation variation. Binding-point bias remains a separate component with a separate growth requirement.
chapters.scope: The result is tied to the declared loss and regularity conditions. It is not a universal theorem for all nonsmooth M-estimators.

chapters.title: Generated Responses, Estimated Operators, and Noisy Derivatives
chapters.overview: Estimated derivatives and operators carry first-stage error into spectra, bridges, and counterfactual maps. Same-sample covariance, local range stability, noise-square bias, and moving frames must enter the expansion. Sample splitting solves only the terms its independence structure addresses.
chapters.method: Let two independent estimates of a derivative share the same conditional mean. Show that their symmetrized cross-product removes the noise-square term that contaminates a naive Gram matrix. Test local bridge stability with a map such as A(eta) = (1, eta^2).
chapters.exercise: Compare naive Gram, split Gram, and estimated transport under independent and shared first-stage samples. Track bias, covariance, subspace error, and range residuals.
chapters.checkpoint: State which bias or dependence term each split removes. Cross-fitting does not by itself establish range membership or operator stability.
chapters.scope: The chapter develops expansions for the generated objects used here. General double or debiased machine learning lies outside its boundary.

chapters.title: Inference for Rank, Singular Values, and Eigenspaces
chapters.overview: Exact rank, numerical rank, and effective rank answer different questions. Perturbation bounds transfer matrix error into singular-value and subspace error only when separation conditions hold. Near ties and lower-rank strata require set-valued or threshold-aware reporting.
chapters.method: Apply a matrix-error bound to singular values and an eigengap bound to subspaces. Let the gap shrink and identify which orientation or rank statements cease to be stable, while value-based risk bounds may remain meaningful.
chapters.exercise: Use the same estimation noise on separated, nearly tied, and exactly lower-rank matrices. Compare estimated singular values, subspace angles, and threshold decisions.
chapters.checkpoint: A small positive estimated singular value is evidence about a noisy matrix; a new identified direction requires uncertainty analysis and a declared threshold.
chapters.scope: The chapter covers perturbation and rank-inference boundaries needed by the frontiers. General random matrix theory is omitted.

chapters.title: Local Projections and Covariance for Dependent Data
chapters.overview: A local-projection result is defined by its horizon, outcome unit, shock normalization, controls, sample, and covariance estimator. Serial, spatial, and clustered dependence call for different sandwich constructions. Robustness means stability across declared protocols, not silent changes in scale.
chapters.method: Write the score sandwich for a simple horizon-specific projection and construct a HAC covariance estimator. Rescale the shock and derive the corresponding transformation of coefficients, standard errors, and cumulative responses.
chapters.exercise: Generate serial, spatial, and cluster-correlated errors. Compare iid, HAC, spatial-HAC, and cluster standard errors under one fixed response definition.
chapters.checkpoint: Record basis points, annualization, calendar aggregation, and shock scaling before comparing two response estimates.
chapters.scope: The focus is covariance and normalization for applied local projections. A full catalogue of time-series models is unnecessary.

chapters.title: Dependent Bootstraps and Nonsmooth Frontiers
chapters.overview: Block and multiplier resampling must reproduce the relevant dependence and rerun generated stages. Minima, maxima, ties, and boundaries can be only directionally differentiable. Interior regularity, boundary inference, and fallback projection methods therefore belong to separate branches of the procedure.
chapters.method: Use the minimum of two smooth functions to derive a directional derivative at a tie. Compare that map with an interior case, then specify which first-stage estimates and optimization steps must be repeated inside every bootstrap draw.
chapters.exercise: Evaluate naive plug-in intervals and full re-estimation intervals in interior, boundary, and tie designs. Report empirical coverage in the synthetic experiment.
chapters.checkpoint: Visual plausibility of a bootstrap distribution is a diagnostic. Coverage requires a resampling argument matched to the statistic and dependence structure.
chapters.scope: The chapter treats nonsmooth counterfactual frontiers and their regularity conditions. It does not state a universal directional-bootstrap theorem.

chapters.title: Predictive Validation, Coordinate Selection, and Oracle Bounds
chapters.overview: Prediction exercises require chronological splits, separation of selection and evaluation, explicit baselines, and finite candidate classes. Oracle inequalities bound selection error under stated conditions, while cross-fitting controls reuse of estimated geometry. Predictive success remains evidence about the declared forecast task.
chapters.method: Prove a basic oracle inequality for empirical risk minimization over a finite dictionary and display the nuisance-error term. Identify how using future information changes both the selected candidate and the validity of the bound.
chapters.exercise: Compare a leakage-prone random split with a proper out-of-time split in a synthetic archive or backlog problem. Report baseline loss, selection uncertainty, and held-out performance.
chapters.checkpoint: Describe a held-out RMSE gain on its prediction task. Causal identification and performance in untested environments require additional designs.
chapters.scope: The chapter covers finite dictionaries, temporal validation, and nuisance-aware selection. General boosting, deep learning, and learning theory are excluded.
